This absolutely should never be translated as “formation” or “fabrication”. Rather, it is something like “former” or “fabricator” or “producer”.
Reasons:
1) Per the Khajjaniya sutta: “And why, monks, do you call them ‘saṅkhāras’? Because they produce produced things, monks, that is why they are called ‘saṅkhāras’.”
2) They are called {'du byed} in Tibetan. {byed} is an agentive ending in Tibetan grammar, analogous to the English suffix “-er” or “-or”, and is contrasted with the patientive ending {byas}. Cf. saṃskṛta {'dus byas} “produced thing”.
3) Miphams Khejuk says “{rnam shes la yang srid kyi sa bon 'debs pas 'du byed ces bya ste/}” i.e. “Because they plant the seed of rebirth in one’s consciousness, they are called ‘producers.’ “
4) The illustrative example for saṃskāras in the {bka' gdams pha chos/} is a potter. The text says “{'du byed dag ni rdza mkhan bzhin/}” i.e. “Producers are like a potter.” Potters are producers, not products.
Therefore, this does not mean “formation”.

1) (noun) Tibetan Royal Year; the Tibetan lunisolar year. The first year of this system began in 127 BCE, which is when the Tibetan Emperor Nyatri Tsenpo ascended to the throne. So, the current Tibetan Royal Year can be roughly calculated by adding 127 to the current Gregorian year. However, because it is a lunisolar calendar, it rolls over to a new year at {lo sar}, not at the Gregorian new year. This means that the first month or two of the Gregorian calendar are still part of the previous Gregorian year’s corresponding Tibetan Royal Year.\n2) (sentence) “May Tibet Be Victorious!”, a common patriotic cry.
